issues.legal_issue: A court exercising discretionary writ jurisdiction may refuse relief where a claimant has brought an inordinate and unexplained challenge after delay that has affected other parties' rights.
material_facts: The claimants challenged a property declaration made decades earlier, and the later writ petition initially did not seek to quash that declaration; that relief was added by amendment years after the petition was filed.

The petition did not give a satisfactory explanation for the delay. The claimants relied on repeated representations and proceedings before authorities, including attempts to obtain relief through remedies that did not provide the relief sought.
Property had meanwhile been allotted to displaced persons, and subsequent purchasers and other third-party interests had arisen.
issues.conclusion: The High Court ought not to have entertained the writ petition or granted relief because the delay was inordinate and unexplained and affected third-party rights.
issues.legal_principle: Delay and laches are matters of judicial discretion rather than an inflexible rule of law. The court considers the length of delay, the explanation for it, conduct during the interval, and whether rights accrued to others. Repeated representations or pursuit of remedies not provided by law do not, without more, satisfactorily explain delay. The Court relied on Lindsay Petroleum Company v. Prosper Armstrong Hurd, approved in Moon Mills Ltd. v. Industrial Courts and Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation v. Balwant Regular Motor Service; Amrit Lal Berry v. CCE; State of Maharashtra v. Digambar; Shiv Dass v. Union of India; City and Industrial Development Corporation v. Dosu Aardeshir Bhiwandiwala; State of M.P. v. Nandlal Jaiswal; Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Company Ltd. v. District Board, Bhojpur; and Municipal Council v. Shaha Hyder Baig.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_challenge and inordinate_delay and not satisfactory_explanation and (wrong_or_incomplete_remedies or third_party_rights_accrued)

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A claimant asks a court to exercise its discretionary public-law jurisdiction to remedy an alleged legal wrong.
predicates.inordinate_delay: The claimant waits an exceptionally long time after the challenged action before seeking effective judicial relief.
predicates.satisfactory_explanation: The claimant sets out a substantiated and legally adequate explanation for failing to seek relief earlier.
predicates.wrong_or_incomplete_remedies: The claimant spends time pursuing representations or procedures that cannot grant the relief ultimately sought, or seeks relief that does not effectively challenge the action at issue.
predicates.third_party_rights_accrued: Rights or interests of other persons arise during the claimant's delay.

issues.definition: When a claimant brings an exceptionally late writ challenge without a satisfactory explanation, and pursues ineffective remedies or allows other persons' rights to arise during the delay, the court may refuse writ relief.

issues.legal_issue: A final judgment rejecting a challenge to an action cannot be circumvented by a later writ petition seeking to reopen the same issue.
material_facts: An earlier writ petition by one of the original owners' legal representatives challenged the property declaration and was dismissed, including on the ground that the challenge was belated.
That judgment was not appealed and attained finality.
Other legal representatives later pursued proceedings that again challenged the same declaration, and the later writ petition sought to reopen that issue.
The earlier petitioner and the later claimants were co-owners or legal representatives of the same owners.
issues.conclusion: The later writ petition could not reopen the issue concluded by the earlier final judgment; the judgment also bound the authorities, and the earlier proceeding was not confined to a ruling on alternative remedy alone.
issues.legal_principle: A judgment must be read as a whole in its factual context, and a final judgment may not be ignored or reopened in a later proceeding on the same issue. This ruling was based on finality and judicial propriety, not on a holding that the doctrine of res judicata applied. The Court relied on Shakur Basti Shamshan Bhumi Sudhar Samiti v. Lt. Governor, A.P. Housing Board v. Mohd. Sadatullah, Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. v. Gopal Krishna Sengupta, Food Corporation of India v. S.N. Nagarkar, Oriental Bank of Commerce v. Sunder Lal Jain, India Household and Healthcare Ltd. v. LG Household and Healthcare Ltd., U.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. Assistant Commissioner of Police (Traffic), and A. Viswanath Pillai v. Special Tahsildar for Land Acquisition No. IV. It explained that the earlier judgment rejected the challenge both because an available remedy had not been used and because the challenge was brought belatedly.

predicates.subsequent_writ_proceeding: A claimant brings a later writ proceeding after an earlier judicial proceeding concerning the challenged action.
predicates.prior_final_judgment: A competent court has issued a judgment on the issue and that judgment has attained finality.
predicates.same_issue_reopened: The later proceeding again seeks judicial determination of the issue already concluded.

issues.definition: A later writ proceeding cannot reopen an issue that a final judgment in an earlier proceeding has already concluded.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant may not raise in a later writ proceeding a ground that was available but omitted from an earlier proceeding based on the same cause of action.
material_facts: The claimants had an earlier writ proceeding challenging the property declaration.
The contention that the required notice procedure had not been followed was available to them in the earlier proceeding but was not raised there.
They later sought to raise that contention in a subsequent writ petition by amendment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in allowing the omitted ground to be raised and decided in the later proceeding because the ground was barred by principles analogous to constructive res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Constructive res judicata in writ proceedings prevents a party from taking successive proceedings on the same cause of action and raising grounds that could and should have been raised earlier. The Court relied on Devilal Modi, Proprietor, M/s Daluram Pannalal Modi v. Sales Tax Officer, Ratlam.

rule.if: later_writ_proceeding and same_cause_of_action and ground_available_earlier and not ground_raised_earlier

predicates.later_writ_proceeding: A claimant brings a writ proceeding after an earlier writ proceeding involving the challenged action.
predicates.same_cause_of_action: The later proceeding seeks relief based on the same underlying challenged action as the earlier proceeding.
predicates.ground_available_earlier: The factual or legal ground relied on in the later proceeding could have been raised in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.ground_raised_earlier: The claimant actually raised that ground in the earlier proceeding.

issues.definition: When a claimant brings a later writ proceeding on the same cause of action, a ground available but omitted from the earlier proceeding cannot be raised later.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on ordinary civil-court jurisdiction does not itself bar constitutional writ review of a custodian's determination, including where disputed facts arise.
material_facts: The challenged determination concerned whether property was evacuee property, a matter assigned to the custodian under the governing legislation.
The legislation barred civil courts from deciding that matter, while providing administrative remedies against the custodian's decision.
The claimants sought review of the determination through a constitutional writ petition.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to entertain a writ petition challenging the custodian's proceedings, even though the issue involved disputed facts and civil-court jurisdiction was barred.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory exclusion of civil-court jurisdiction does not oust the High Court's constitutional jurisdiction. A writ court may, in an appropriate case and in its discretion, decide disputed questions of fact; there is no absolute bar. The Court relied on Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab v. Jafran Begum, a three-Judge Bench decision, as well as State of Orissa v. Dr. (Miss) Binapani Dei, Smt. Gunwant Kaur v. Municipal Committee, Bhatinda, Om Prakash v. State of Haryana, and ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. The relevant statutory provisions discussed were Sections 28 and 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act and Section 36 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A claimant asks a High Court to review an alleged legal wrong under its constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.civil_court_jurisdiction_barred: A law excludes ordinary civil courts from deciding the subject matter of the dispute.
predicates.custodian_determination_challenged: The claimant challenges a determination by an authority empowered to decide whether property has a special statutory status.

issues.definition: When a claimant challenges a custodian's determination through constitutional writ proceedings, exclusion of ordinary civil-court jurisdiction does not by itself prevent the High Court from reviewing it.

issues.legal_issue: A writ court may decide disputed facts in an appropriate case, but it must not substitute unsupported factual findings for the decision of the statutory authority or treat itself as an appellate tribunal.
material_facts: The parties disputed title to the land, whether a court auction had transferred ownership, and whether interested persons had received notice before the property was declared evacuee property.
The records from the relevant period and the records of the alleged execution proceedings were unavailable, and neither side produced material establishing the disputed events.
The High Court nevertheless found that no lawful auction had occurred and that required notice had not been given.
Revenue records showed the alleged purchaser's name before the declaration and the custodian's name afterward; the claimants bore the burden of proving their asserted title and interest.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's findings that no auction had occurred and that required notice had not been given were unsupported and inappropriate; the Court rejected those findings and also rejected the Collector-cum-Deputy Custodian's contrary conclusion on ownership.
issues.legal_principle: A writ court does not sit in appeal over an authority's decision. It may intervene for want or excess of jurisdiction, an apparent error of law, absence of legal evidence, or perversity. It may decline to decide complicated factual issues, although whether to do so is a matter of discretion rather than jurisdiction. A factual conclusion about notice or title must be supported by material; the claimant bears the burden of proving the asserted title, right, and interest. The Court relied on Surya Dev Rai v. Ramchander Rai, Ranjeet Singh v. Ravi Prakash, Karnataka State Industrial Investment and Development Corporation Ltd. v. Cavalet India Ltd., Binapani Dei, Gunwant Kaur, Om Prakash, and ABL International.

rule.if: writ_review_of_administrative_decision and disputed_complex_facts and no_supporting_material and unsupported_factual_finding_made

predicates.writ_review_of_administrative_decision: A claimant asks a writ court to review a decision made by a statutory authority.
predicates.disputed_complex_facts: The dispute depends on contested factual matters that require evidence or examination of records.
predicates.no_supporting_material: The party relying on a factual assertion produces no material capable of establishing it.
predicates.unsupported_factual_finding_made: The writ court makes a decisive factual finding despite the absence of supporting material.

issues.definition: When a writ court reviews an administrative decision involving complex disputed facts, it may not make a decisive factual finding unsupported by evidence or records.

issues.legal_issue: A property declaration made under the evacuee-property legislation remains valid where the challenger fails to establish that the declaration was procedurally unlawful.
material_facts: The property was declared evacuee property after the authority issued notices to the alleged evacuees and published a public notice, according to the State's account and the contemporaneous declaration process.
The challengers asserted that they had not received notice and that the alleged prior owner had never acquired the land through execution of a money decree.
The records needed to determine whether notice had been issued or whether an execution auction had occurred were unavailable, and the challengers produced no material establishing their assertions.
Revenue records identified the alleged purchaser before the declaration and the custodian after it.
A prior final judgment had rejected a belated challenge to the declaration.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the declaration of the land as evacuee property was valid in law and rejected the High Court's findings of manifest illegality and failure to give notice.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 7 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, the custodian may declare property evacuee property after forming the required opinion, giving notice in the prescribed manner to interested persons, and holding such inquiry as the circumstances permit. The procedure is mandatory. Whether property vested in the custodian is a question of fact, reviewable only in exceptional circumstances, including violation of natural justice. The challenger must support allegations of lack of notice or title with material. The Court relied on Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab v. Jafran Begum, Ebrahim Aboobaker v. Tek Chand Dolwani, and Nasir Ahmed v. Assistant Custodian General, Evacuee Property.

predicates.property_status_declaration_challenged: A claimant asks a court to invalidate an official declaration that property has a special statutory status.
predicates.no_material_proving_procedural_illegalit: The claimant produces no evidence establishing that the required procedure was not followed.
predicates.prior_final_judgment_rejected_challenge: A final earlier judgment rejected a challenge to the same declaration.

issues.definition: A challenged property-status declaration is upheld where the claimant produces no material proving procedural illegality and a final earlier judgment has rejected the challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition of property validly declared evacuee property vests it in the central government and ends its status as evacuee property and the custodian's authority over it.
material_facts: The property had been validly declared evacuee property.
The central government published a notification under the displaced-persons legislation acquiring the property for rehabilitation purposes.
The property was acquired and allotted for the rehabilitation of displaced persons.
issues.conclusion: Upon publication of the acquisition notification, the property vested absolutely in the central government, ceased to be evacuee property, and was no longer subject to the custodian's powers under the evacuee-property legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1) and (2) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 authorizes acquisition of evacuee property for the specified public purpose and provides that publication extinguishes the evacuee's right, title, and interest and vests the property absolutely in the central government free from encumbrances. Such acquisition requires that the property be evacuee property. The consequence is to divest the custodian of the rights arising from vesting under the evacuee-property legislation. The Court relied on Major Gopal Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property; Basant Ram v. Union of India; Dafedar Niranjan Singh v. Custodian, Evacuee Property; Haji Siddik Haji Umar v. Union of India; and Dr. Zafar Ali Shah v. Assistant Custodian of Evacuee Property.

predicates.valid_evacuee_property_declaration: The property has been validly declared to have the statutory status that permits its acquisition for displaced-person rehabilitation.
predicates.central_government_acquisition_notificat: The central government publishes a notification acquiring the property for rehabilitation purposes.

issues.definition: When property has been validly declared evacuee property and the central government publishes an acquisition notification, the property vests in the central government and ceases to have evacuee status.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional authority may revise only orders made by the categories of officers specified in its empowering provision.
material_facts: The Chief Settlement Commissioner purported to revise an order made by a Collector-cum-Deputy Custodian under the evacuee-property legislation.
The empowering provision authorized revision of orders made by specified settlement officers and related officers under the displaced-persons legislation.
The Collector-cum-Deputy Custodian whose order was revised was not among the officers specified in that provision.
issues.conclusion: The Chief Settlement Commissioner lacked jurisdiction to revise the Collector-cum-Deputy Custodian's order, and the purported revisional order was non-est in law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 24 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 gives the Chief Settlement Commissioner revisional power over orders of the officers named in that section. Its plain language does not authorize revision of an order made by an officer acting under the separate evacuee-property legislation who is not among those named.

predicates.revisional_authority_exercises_power: An authority purports to revise an order under a statutory revisional power.
predicates.challenged_order_made_by_officer_outside: The order being revised was made by an officer who is not within the categories of decision-makers covered by the revisional power.

issues.definition: A revisional order is without jurisdiction when the authority uses its revisional power to review an order made by an officer outside the categories covered by that power.
